# How to Get Inventory for an Online Boutique: Complete Guide

Running an online


[clothing boutique](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/apparel/) is both a high-potential standalone business and a powerful digital extension for an existing storefront. Whether you’re launching an e-commerce brand from scratch or expanding your brick-and-mortar store into omnichannel retail, success depends on the same foundation: getting the right products on your digital shelves.


However, unless you plan on manufacturing your own stock, you’ll need to source your boutique inventory from wholesalers and other creators. While established shop owners may already have vendor relationships, sourcing for e-commerce brings new considerations around margins, drop dates and fulfillment. We’ll show you how to navigate it all in this guide on how to get inventory for your online boutique.


- Where to get inventory for an online boutique
- How to vet suppliers
- How to choose the right inventory
- How to store and organize your inventory
- How to set prices
- How to sync inventory across channels

From managing always-evolving inventory to making personal connections during sales, your clothing store needs tools that help you do it all.

## Where to get inventory for an online boutique


Whether you’re sourcing your very first collection or an established store owner expanding into ecommerce, you have several primary paths to acquire inventory:


1. Attending trade shows


2. Working with online wholesale suppliers


3. Working directly with manufacturers


4. Visiting offline wholesalers


5. Using wholesale directories


6. Reselling used goods


### 1. Fashion & apparel trade shows


If you want to touch fabrics, inspect stitching and meet brand reps face-to-face, nothing beats hitting the trade show floor.


Apparel trade shows are essentially giant industry expos where brands and manufacturers show off their upcoming collections before they hit the market. While a few open their doors to the public, most are strictly B2B—meaning you’ll need to prove you’re an actual retail buyer (usually just by showing a business card, resale license or your registered store name) to get a badge.


**PROS** : You get to vet product quality with your own eyes and hands, which saves you from unpleasant fabric or sizing surprises down the road. It’s also the fastest way to build real, personal relationships with brand reps, which often opens the door to better terms, lower minimum orders and faster replenishment later on.


**CONS** : They aren’t cheap. Between flights, hotels, and registration fees, traveling to a show adds up quickly. Plus, because they only run for a couple of days a few times a year, you have to plan your buying calendar around their schedule, not yours.


Some of the most popular trade shows for wholesale boutique clothing are:


- [ASD Market Week](https://asdonline.com/) : ASD is a massive trade show held twice a year in Las Vegas. It connects retailers to thousands of worldwide brands, including apparel.


- [COTERIE](https://www.coteriefashionevents.com/en/home.html) : This show connects the best brands in women’s fashion, including apparel, accessories and footwear, with buyers from around the world in New York City and online. COTERIE also has an annual show dedicated to swimwear and resort wear in Miami.


- [Designers & Agents](http://designersandagents.com/) : Designers & Agents showcases a curated selection of 300 designers every season in New York and Los Angeles.


- [MAGIC](https://www.magicfashionevents.com/) : This wholesale trade show specializes in exhibiting the latest trends in contemporary clothing for women and men. They have shows several times a year in different locations across the United States, including New York City, Las Vegas and Nashville.


- [NY NOW](https://nynow.com/) : Based in New York twice a year, this event features educational panels and wholesale connections alike.


- [Pure London](https://www.purelondon.com/about-pure-london) : This London-based fashion trade show showcases womenswear, menswear and kidswear brands twice a year.


### 2. Wholesale buying platforms


If traveling to a trade show isn’t an option, you can also source inventory for your online boutique via wholesale buying platforms. These are ecommerce sites that specialize in selling in bulk to businesses (B2B) rather than direct to consumers (DTC), and so tend to have much higher minimum orders.


Just as you would at a trade show, you’ll probably need to prove that you’re a fashion buyer to gain access to wholesale inventory and pricing.


**PROS** : Online wholesale marketplaces offer a wider range than trade shows—if you want to sell it, someone online probably has it. You also don’t need to travel to attend shows, can buy inventory for your online boutique whenever you need it and can often get the best prices online.


**CONS** : Buying inventory online can be a little riskier than buying in-person at trade shows. Unless the wholesaler or marketplace carefully curates their brands, you won’t know the quality of the items until you receive them, and there are a number of scam sites out there you need to avoid. To mitigate disappointment, see if the wholesalers offer samples.


Check out these wholesale buying websites to get started:


- [NuOrder by Lightspeed](https://www.nuorder.com/) – NuOrder is a wholesale buying platform with both free and paid plans to help you buy from curated brands you know you can trust. Womenswear, menswear, kidswear, home goods, accessories and beauty products are all available for a wide selection.


- [LA Showroom](https://www.lashowroom.com/) – This online wholesaler sells a wide variety of womenswear, menswear, kidswear, footwear, beauty products and accessories.


- [FashionGo](https://www.fashiongo.net/) – FashionGo is a well-established site that offers everything from kidswear and fragrances to women’s fashions.


- [Magnolia Fashion Wholesale](https://magnoliafashionwholesale.com/) – This Miami-based wholesaler specializes in contemporary womenswear and offers shipping to 80 countries.


- [LuxiSoCool](https://www.luxisocool.com/) – LuxiSoCool offers wholesale fashion packs curated by their in-house stylists, so you can get a selection of coordinated styles for your chosen demographic.


### 3. Work with manufacturers


Instead of or in addition to working with wholesalers you can work directly with manufacturers to get inventory for your online boutique. You can either buy pre-made goods directly from them, cutting out the wholesaler middleman, or you can order custom inventory.


If you find products you like at other online shops, look for a manufacturer or brand name in the product description. Research the brand and contact them directly to see if they offer wholesale pricing.


**PROS** : Cutting out the wholesaler middleman can lower inventory acquisitions costs. If you decide to make custom merchandise with a manufacturer, you’ll have unique stock no one else is carrying.


**CONS** : Wholesalers exist for a reason. Manufacturers generally specialize in producing products—not selling them. Not all manufacturers are willing to sell directly to retailers or have an easy way for you to order. If you do decide to buy directly from the manufacturer, you’ll run into the same relationship barriers as working with a wholesaler. And if you’re ordering custom products, be sure to budget for design and sample costs.


### 4. Offline wholesale clothing vendors


Offline wholesalers are a lot like trade shows, but they’re open all year. They function similarly to trade shows—you’ll go to test quality in person and make connections face to face. If you’re lucky enough to live near one, you can visit regularly to source inventory for your online boutique.


**PROS** :


All the benefits of trade shows, but open all year. That means you can fit visits into your schedule as needed.


**CONS** :


If you’re not in a major market area for a year-round wholesale market, you’ll still need to pay travel costs to get there. Also, not all suppliers exhibit year-round at fixed markets.


Some of the biggest offline wholesale vendor markets include:


- [AmericasMart Atlanta](https://www.americasmart.com/) – Claims to be the world’s largest collection of wholesale gift, decor and apparel showrooms. Has both permanent showrooms and rotating speciality markets.


- [Dallas Market Center](https://dallasmarketcenter.com/) – Another large market with both permanent showrooms and rotating speciality markets. In addition to apparel and accessories, you can find housewares, gifts, jewelry and childrens’ goods.


### 5. Wholesaler directories


Wholesale directories are online or printed databases of B2B suppliers, manufacturers and distributors. Unlike online marketplaces or wholesale buying platforms, they don’t process orders or transactions, acting like more of a research and discovery tool that helps connect buyers and sellers. They may be updated weekly, monthly, quarterly or yearly.


**PROS** :


You can browse the catalogs at your leisure, in your own home or office. They’re full of vetted suppliers you know you can trust for your online boutique inventory.


**CONS** :


You usually have to pay a fee to subscribe to these directories. And because these aren’t buying platforms, you’ll still need to build relationships with the vendors you find here before you can start actually placing orders.


If you want to browse some trade catalogs and directories, you can try:


- [Worldwide Brands](https://www.worldwidebrands.com/) – an online directory of wholesalers who work with ecommerce retailers. There’s a one-time fee to sign up, after which you get lifetime access to their vetted suppliers (updated weekly).


- [Wholesale Central](https://www.wholesalecentral.com/index.htm) – a free directory of trusted suppliers with links to their sites for purchasing.


### 6. Fashion resale


Wholesalers are the most common way to get inventory for online boutiques, but they’re not the only way. With thrifting and vintage on the rise, fashion resale could be a viable option for your online clothing store.


**PROS** :


You’ll have a wholly unique inventory that’s attractive to a dedicated subset of customers.


**CONS** :


Sourcing high quality clothing for resale can be far more difficult than working with wholesalers, and may include long hours networking at yard sales and estate sales. You still need to make connections, but this time with individuals instead of companies.


## **How to vet wholesale suppliers**


Placing your first order with a new supplier can be nerve-racking, as with anything that involves money and risk. Even if you have years of experience with local vendors, branching into new digital wholesale suppliers requires a strict vetting process to protect your delivery timelines and margins.


Here are a few measures you can take to ensure you’re working with trustworthy wholesalers and manufacturers:


### Get references


Ask the supplier for references, then contact those references and ask them how they like working with the supplier. Ask them how long they’ve been working with the supplier, what the supplier’s lead times are like, if they are reliable and if there have been any specific challenges or issues. If the supplier isn’t willing to hand over references, that’s a red flag. It may mean they don’t have many, or any, satisfied retailers.


### Get to know your contacts


As you’re vetting a particular supplier, find out if you’ll be working with a dedicated sales rep—without a dedicated representative, your requests may slip under the radar.


If you do have a dedicated sales rep, pay attention to their communication style and responsiveness. If they often don’t have the answers you need or take days to respond to an email, working with them is likely to be pretty frustrating. If they respond promptly and are organized, then you could be looking at the beginning of a strong partnership.


### Look at samples—real samples


Photos are nice, but they don’t give you the tactile experience you need to properly evaluate a product. Before ordering inventory in bulk for an online boutique, you need to see and touch some physical samples.


If you’re able to, visit the supplier’s warehouse. While you’re there, visually inspect and feel the products for quality, as well as observe the general conditions and organization of the facility. If you can’t make the trip, ask for samples to be mailed to you. (You may need to pay for shipping.) Ask for photos of the warehouse and how inventory is stored before shipping.


For more tips, check out our guide on[how to buy wholesale](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/how-to-buy-wholesale/) .


## How to choose the right inventory for your online boutique


Curating a great assortment takes more than good taste—it takes a clear buying strategy. Whether you’re taking an existing storefront online or launching a digital-first brand, evaluate these core factors before placing your wholesale orders:


- Define your target customer
- Choose a niche
- Calculate target margins
- Build a strategic pricing model
- Build a balanced assortment
- Track demand and market trends
- Plan for seasonality
- Factor in vendor lead times


### Define your target customer


It’s a good idea to build detailed buyer personas including demographics, buying power and style preferences. Knowing exactly who you’re buying for helps keep your catalog focused so you only order items your target customers would actually pay for.


### Choose a niche


Define a clear niche to cater to specific customer preferences rather than competing directly with generalists and e-com giants. Tailoring your catalog to an underserved market creates a stronger brand identity and can help build long-term customer loyalty.


### Calculate target margins


Work out your target profit margins early to make sure every item you bring into your store can generate healthy net revenue. Aim for a minimum 50% to 60% gross profit margin on apparel to ensure that each sale covers your[Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-cogs/) and overhead costs.


Remember that your COGS isn’t just what you paid the supplier for the product, it includes all costs related to acquiring, preparing and landing inventory so it’s ready for sale. It does not include operating expenses.


Exact line items may vary depending on the nature of your business. For example, a brick-and-mortar store expanding online will factor in landed freight and physical shrinkage across locations, while a dropshipper or online-only boutique may only have to factor in wholesale costs, custom packaging and import duties.

### Build a balanced assortment


To balance your product mix and avoid tying up too much capital in slow-moving inventory or deadstock, we recommend the 60/30/10 inventory framework. Essentially, this framework divides your assortment or Open-to-Buy (OTB) budget into three categories: core products, seasonal/trendy items and statement pieces.


Here’s the breakdown:


**Core products** **Seasonal/Trendy** **Statement/Experimental**


What’s included


Everyday wear, classic styles with steady turnover and low risk—your “bread and butter” inventory.


Mid-tier popular styles, seasonal items, breakout models that create interest and satisfy emerging demand.


High-impact/high-margin products, luxury goods, experimental styles that give your assortment some personality but typically have low turnover.

### Track demand and market trends


Skip the guesswork and let actual sales data and search volume dictate what you restock. Tracking customer engagement, social media trends and sell-through rates helps you spot breakout styles early and restock best-sellers before interest cools. Buying platforms like NuORDER by Lightspeed also provide insights into[market trends](https://helpdesk.nuorder.com/hc/en-us/articles/27071765927195-Order-Trends-overview#h_01JNHB0MKT46EEP20TXES39JJZ) such as top products and categories by brand.


### Plan for seasonality


Timing is everything in retail. Aligning your product drops with weather shifts, holidays and fashion cycles ensures new arrivals hit your site right when customer buying intent peaks. Getting seasonal stock on the floor early keeps items moving at full retail price, saving you from having to run steep markdowns to clear slow-moving inventory later on.


### Factor in vendor lead times


Retail may move fast, but wholesale supply chains don’t. Most wholesale suppliers require 60 to 90 days lead time for production and shipping, so you’ll want to place your seasonal orders roughly two to three months ahead of your target drop date. Building in that extra buffer ensures your collections land in your warehouse right on schedule so you never miss a prime shopping window.


## **How to store and organize your inventory**


Once you’ve got your inventory, now you need to organize it so you can sell it without wasting hours on extra admin tasks. Here are a few pointers that will help you organize, store and ship your inventory to make your life easier, and keep your customers happy.


### 1. Organizing your boutique’s inventory


The key to well-organized inventory is creating a system and using software to keep track of stock, sizes,[stock-keeping units (SKUs)](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/sku-numbers/) , sales and more.


When you use a retail POS with[connected eCom](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/ecommerce/) , you can easily upload your inventory into a centralized dashboard. Whenever you make a sale, quantities are automatically updated and you’re notified, so that you can jump to the fulfillment process.


### 2. Storing your online boutique’s inventory


Where you store your inventory depends entirely on your setup. If you run an existing retail store, your stockroom is already your distribution center—you’ll just need dedicated shelving or bins for items allocated to digital orders.


If you’re running a boutique strictly online, the advantage is zero storefront overhead: you can start by storing inventory in a clean, dedicated room at home and scale into a third-party logistics (3PL) warehouse or storage facility as volume grows.


You’ll need shelves and bins for dedicated storage. Look for clear bins that close, so that you can easily see your inventory and protect it from getting damaged, wet or mildewy. Create a labeling system for your bins and items. Add SKUs to your ecommerce software and add these labels to your inventory to make them easy to find.


### 3. Shipping inventory


When a customer makes a purchase, your[ecommerce software](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/ecom/) will notify you. Then it’s time to package and ship the order. Keep shipping materials on hand. Stock up on poly mailers, boxes, tissue paper, plastic apparel sleeves and packing tape.


To save time at the post office, get a scale and shipping label printer. Look for fulfillment tools that integrate with your ecommerce software to import orders and print labels in bulk, and automatically send customers shipping notifications and tracking information.


## **How to set prices for your online boutique**


There are a few different ways to set prices for an online boutique. The first is the **keystone pricing** method—setting your retail price to double the wholesale cost (2x markup)—because it’s easy to implement and builds in a 50% gross margin for every product.


Unfortunately, keystone pricing only factors in wholesale cost—ignoring variables like demand, competition and perceived value. This can easily lead to underpricing premium products and leaving money on the table, or overpricing common items and losing sales to cheaper competitors. It also doesn’t account for shipping, overhead, duties, taxes and other costs related to running your business, so at the end of the day, that 50% gross margin might not even keep you out of the red.


The second method is to use the **manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP)** , the name that the manufacturer recommends you sell the item for. Some manufacturers mandate an MSRP, which doesn’t take your costs into account. Other manufacturers simply offer the MSRP as a suggestion, to help put their retailers on a level playing field.


The third strategy is to use the **absorption pricing method** , which involves adding up the costs incurred to run your business (including labor, marketing, software and the cost of your inventory), dividing it by the number of units purchased and adding your desired profit margin.


## **How to sync your online inventory with other sales channels**


Managing disconnected inventory systems is a recipe for duplicate sales and inventory headaches. Multi-channel syncing ensures that when an item sells in one place, it updates everywhere.


If you have a brick-and-mortar store and you’re expanding into ecom, the first thing you need is for your point of sale and ecommerce platform to communicate. In order of convenience, you can:


1. **Use an omnichannel platform** . This is where you use one provider for your[retail POS system](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/) and your ecommerce platform, like Lightspeed Retail connected to Lightspeed eCom. The systems are made to work with each other, so you’ll be able to manage inventory, customers and data from one platform.
2. **Integrate with a supported platform** . This is where you use a supported partner and integrate with your point of sale. You’re working with two different companies, but the systems easily integrate and should communicate with each other. As they’re made by different developers, they might not have matching features. For example, you might need to do some work to make sure your loyalty program is functioning right.
3. **Have a connection built for you** . if no integration between your chosen POS and ecommerce platforms exist, you can have one built for you. This will almost certainly be expensive and time consuming, so you’ll nearly always be better off looking for a different solution.


### Place orders


When you have a connected system, you can place orders for online inventory and in-store inventory at the same time. Using Lightspeed, you can make sure you’re ordering the right amount of inventory for your online boutique using automated reorder points, demand forecasting tools and the recommended reorder report. It will crunch the numbers based on sales data and let you know what’s hot and needs more stock.


### Train employees


If you have staff running a retail storefront, having your online catalog connected to your POS means your store team can fulfill orders directly from your floor or backroom during downtime. You’ll need to train them on how often to check for sales, your practices for taking stock off the sales floor or out of your warehouse, how to package online orders and how to manage shipping.


## TL;DR: How to get inventory for an online boutique


Sourcing inventory for an online boutique isn’t something you set and forget—it’s an ongoing balancing act between customer taste, profit margins and supply chain timing.


Whether you’re launching an e-commerce store from your living room or using digital channels to expand an established storefront, your long-term profitability comes down to discipline. Vet your suppliers thoroughly, protect your margins beyond basic keystone markups and use concrete sales data rather than guesswork to drive reorders.


Most importantly, keep your operations connected. When your inventory, sales channels and fulfillment workflows communicate through a centralized platform, you spend less time untangling stock counts and more time building the collections that keep customers coming back.

## FAQs about getting inventory for an online boutique


### How much inventory should I start with for an online boutique?


There isn’t a single rule, but many new online boutiques start lean with roughly 10 to 30 styles with three to eight units per size or colorway. Starting with conservative quantities allows you to present a complete, cohesive collection without locking up too much capital in untested merchandise before you know what resonates with your audience.


### Can I start an online boutique without buying inventory?


Yes, you can start an online boutique without purchasing upfront inventory by using dropshipping or print-on-demand models. Under these fulfillment models, third-party suppliers hold the stock and ship items directly to your customers whenever an order is placed on your site.


### How do I manage inventory across multiple sales channels?


The best way to manage inventory across multiple sales channels is by using an omnichannel POS and e-commerce platform. Centralizing your stock updates inventory levels automatically across your online store, social media channels and physical locations whenever a sale occurs, helping prevent overselling and excess inventory.


### What is the best way to find reliable clothing wholesalers?


The best channels for sourcing wholesale inventory are verified B2B trade directories, apparel trade shows and direct brand partnerships. When evaluating vendors, prioritize suppliers that offer low minimum order quantities (MOQs), transparent pricing structures and samples so you can inspect product quality firsthand.


### Where do online boutiques get their inventory?


Online boutiques source inventory from online wholesale marketplaces, B2B digital trade directories, trade shows, manufacturers or dropshipping suppliers. Many independent retailers also partner with boutique clothing designers for exclusive, small-batch collections.
